newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - Swiss banks launch asset management school.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Swiss banks launch asset management school.

text.p: Swiss bankers have launched a business school to safeguard the country's position as the world's premier centre for private banking and international asset management.

The idea behind FAME -- the International Centre for Financial Asset Management and Engineering -- is to create a global centre of competence in asset management by attracting top-notch academics and experienced private bankers.
"FAME should become the Bell Laboratory or Silicon Valley of asset management," said Patrick Odier, partner of Geneva-based private bank Lombard Odier & Cie, founded almost 200 years ago.

FAME is a direct response by Swiss bankers to the growing competition they are facing from international competitors who want to muscle in on the traditional strength of Swiss bankers: Managing the assets of wealthy individuals.

"We realised that if we didn't have a commensurate pool of competence here in Switzerland that can bring us up to date at any time on what is being done everywhere in the world in this industry, we will slowly but surely lose our competitive advantage," Odier said.
STUDENTS TO EMULATE STYLE OF SWISS PRIVATE BANKERS
Students at FAME will not only be taught state-of-the-art portolio management, but should also absorb the style of Swiss private bankers, a style Odier compares with that of a doctor.

"When you are very sick you want to see a specialist, but also somebody that can deal with all the personal issues around your sickness. You want somebody to accompany you, to help guide you in the choices you have to make," Odier said.

Fancy sales techniques and smooth talking are of little value unless a private banker can convince a potential client of his loyalty, confidence, trust and the avoidance of conflict of interest at all times.
"Even the brightest finance graduate can't convince an industrialist to hand over his fortune just because of good ideas," Odier said.
Private bankers Lombard Odier, for example, only act as agents for their clients and never take their own position in the market to avoid any hint of conflict of interest.
"At some point you and the client have a position and you want to sell. But which one do you sell first? I don't want to have this problem," he said.
It is this blend of old and new values that Switzerland's private banks see as their continued competitive advantage.
The partners in Lombard Odier, for example, are in daily contact with clients and the specialist teams that manage portfolios so they personally know when problems arise.
"There is no difference in a private bank between labour and capital. There are a number of partners around this table, all of which manage clients," Odier said.
PERSONAL TOUCH DISTINGUISHES PRIVATE BANKS
This personal touch, the essence of the private banking culture, distinguishes private banks from banking officers in large and anonymous international banks.

The Swiss attitude toward confidentiality is another plus in private banking, despite the recent questioning of the whereabouts of assets that were deposited in Swiss banks by Jewish people before or during World War Two.
"Whether it is a private individual, a company or pension fund, we don't think it is useful to talk about your personal matters to anybody else," Odier said.
"Just as you go to a doctor with your own problems, you go to your bank with your own problems."
But the challenges to Switzerland's status as private banker to the world are mounting. Long gone are the days when neutral status, political stability and low taxes guaranteed its role.
Investors, whether private or institutional, no longer accept a lower return on investment just for the sake of having a numbered account in a safe Swiss bank.

State-of-the-art portfolio management at competitive fees is today's hallmark of private bankers in Switzerland, which still manage some $2.4 trillion, or around one-third of the international offshore wealth.
Asset management fees are now between 1.0 to 1.5 percent for private clients with institutions charged less.
"We cannot rest on our laurels, but must learn about what is good in other places rather than observe our magnificent client base grow at a slower rate than in the past," Odier said.
ADDED COMPETITION FROM NEW TECHNOLOGY
In addition to the threat from new competitors, technology is erasing geographical barriers so financial services can be offered to anyone from anywhere.
Odier, 41 and a sixth generation family member in private banking, was one of the driving forces behing the creation of FAME and now chairs its board.
Nothing similar to FAME has ever existed in Switzerland or Europe.
Despite the importance of the banking industry to the Swiss economy, there have not been any academic programmes tailored to asset and portfolio management.
Budding asset managers typically leave universities or other institutions and continue their training in-house at banks, often with highly-qualified teachers and economists.
One of the aims of FAME is to share such knowledge and to speed up the transition between a student leaving university and working as an asset manager.
HOW IT WORKS
FAME is not a traditional school in the sense of having a large campus, but is a virtual learning centre that manages a network of partners and projects from its Geneva headquarters.
"FAME is going to have a very light infrastructure, but a very heavy virtual structure, Odier said.

Professors and leading academics from various partner institutions -- Massachussetts Institute of Technology (MIT), the University of Chicago or New York University (NYU) and others -- will either be brought to FAME or give long-distance classes through the Internet.
Swiss banks -- private and universal -- along with the Universitaire de Haute Etudes Internationale, the Universities of Geneva and Lausanne, and Reuters are among FAME's founders.
FAME, will mainly operate in three areas of activity -- education, training and research.

Programmes start in 1997 and education activities will include a nine-week post graduate specialisation, a diploma in private banking, and the first-ever doctoral programme specialising in asset management.
